newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Red Cross needs money to save soup kitchens.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross needs money to save soup kitchens.

text.p: The Red Cross said on Thursday it was concerned its refugee programmes in the Republic of Yugoslavia would have to be cut back in 1997 because of falling support from donor nations.

"Bosnia-Herzegovina tends to be a high priority for understandable reasons, we are very concerned that Croatia and the federal republic (of Yugoslavia) are being shoved into the background," Daniel Prewitt, head of the Red Cross Bosnia delegation, told Reuters.

Soup kitchens in Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, currently give 30,000 people one hot meal every day and the Red Cross is worried it may have to cut capacity this year because of lack of funds.
"Our biggest concern is the future of the soup kitchens," Hannes Hauksson, head of the Red Cross delegation in the republic of Yugoslavia, told a news conference.

He said the Red Cross was trying to explain the need to donor countries and ensure future support. "It seems that we can't sustain our current concept any more but there may be the possibility to continue with a different model."
However, Hauksson said this would reduce the number of people who benefit from the soup kitchen.
The programme is currently running with a deficit of 1.3 million marks and unless cash pledges equal to that amount are received soon the programme will be forced to close, the Red Cross said.
Prewitt said the forced repatriation of refugees from Western European countries was worrying and the time was not right for so many refugees to return home.

"We are very sensitive to (Western governments') motivation but we feel that it needs to be done in a much more considered manner...I think there's an information gap -- they have not had enough information that clearly defines the extent of the problem," he told Reuters after a news conference.
"It is not just enough for people to come back to reasonably suitable living conditions. There are no jobs and so there's also the issue of economic viability.

"We would like to suggest to governments if they are reinserting large numbers of people into what is already a semi-destabilised society, that could actually be counter-productive to what they want. (It could) further destabilise a situation that the international leadership is committed to stabilising."

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and the Yugoslav Red Cross met in Belgrade to discuss programmes for the former Yugoslavia for 1997 in the face of "chronic decreasing humanitarian aid".
In Yugoslavia there are 556,000 refugees, 400,000 of whom are supported by Red Cross programmes.

"Part of our very key role is to try and prick the conscience of the international community to be re-awakened to a situation that still needs their support," said Renny Nancholas, head of the Red Cross European department.
